  4. Amṛta-pravāha-bhāṣya: we will tell Mahāprabhu that the king behaves like a true Vaiṣṇava, but we will not ask Him to grant the king His darśana.
  5. Verses 20–21 are the king’s own words (first person in the Bengali: muñi, “I”), which Nityānanda repeats. Amṛta-pravāha-bhāṣya: in the western regions such yogīs are called kānphaṭā (“split-eared”) yogīs; they wear a sign made of conch shell in their ears.
  6. Heading in the edition: “Harsh words of the Lord, faithful to the duty of a sannyāsī, as befits an ācārya.”
  7. Amṛta-pravāha-bhāṣya: from the standpoint of the highest goal a sannyāsī incurs fault by meeting a king; and he must avoid the censure of people because his task is to preach dharma, and the preaching of one who is censured does not go well.
  8. Heading in the edition: “Under the guise of respect, a jibe at Dāmodara’s judging what is not his to judge.” Amṛta-pravāha-bhāṣya: the Lord is won by Dāmodara’s devotion, yet his verbal chastisements are often unfitting towards the Lord; by these words the Lord lets it be understood that Dāmodara will have to give up that habit.
  9. Anubhāṣya: You are Īśvara and so are bound to no one; yet by Your own nature You are subject only to the love of Your exclusive (aikāntika) devotees.
  10. Heading in the edition: “Agreeing with the Lord, Nityānanda pleads for the king’s love.”
  11. The Bengali has a singular verb (chāḍileka) and “before her husband” (pati-āge): according to Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam 10.23.34, one of the wives, held back by her husband, gave up her body. Anubhāṣya: see Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, Canto 10, Chapter 23.
  12. The edition reads tāhā pāñā prāṇa rākhe, tomāra āśā dhari’ (with a comma after rākhe); the Bengali and the transliteration follow the edition.
  13. Anubhāṣya: the Lord’s garments, ornaments and all that He uses are eternally non-different from His transcendental body: Śeṣa, a portion of Śrī Baladeva, serves Kṛṣṇa as His bed, garments and so on. Likewise the things used by the guru and the Vaiṣṇavas are non-different from them and eternally worthy of worship.
  14. Anubhāṣya: “I am only a man in the fourth āśrama, not Īśvara; therefore I fear to transgress worldly propriety in body, mind and speech” — that is, “I depend on the opinion of others.” Heading in the edition: “The Lord, as if by a ruse, shows Himself bound by injunctions.”
  15. The edition reads eka ‘rājā’ nāma (without a hyphen); the Bengali and the transliteration follow the edition. Heading in the edition: “The worldly label ‘viṣayī’ destroys every virtue.”
  16. Anubhāṣya: the son is Puruṣottama Jānā (marked with a question mark).

Himself the viṣaya-vigraha, He sees Himself as a gopī and the prince as Vrajendra-nandana Himself; such is the non-dual vision of the pure soul, the “vision of a Vaiṣṇava” (see Madhya 8.277).
  19. Anubhāṣya: the Guṇḍicā temple stands one krośa north-east of the Śrī Mandira; at Ratha-yātrā Śrī Jagannātha goes there for a week and then returns on His chariot. By tradition, Guṇḍicā was the name of King Indradyumna’s queen.

  24. Heading in the edition: “Who has cleaned how much is seen by the amount of dirt gathered.”
  25. Heading in the edition: “The Lord’s own cleaning brought the Guṇḍicā the greatest purity.”
  26. Heading in the edition: “The cleaned and washed temple compared to the pure heart of Śrī Rādhā.”
  27. Anubhāṣya: the Vaiṣṇavas were busy carrying water, while these five — Prabhu Nityānanda, Advaita, Dāmodara-svarūpa, Brahmānanda Bhāratī and Paramānanda Purī — took water together with Mahāprabhu and cleaned the temple.
  28. Anubhāṣya: the one whose service did not please the Lord He chided in a holy way, took by the hand and taught how to serve Kṛṣṇa.
  29. Heading in the edition: “To the good servant the Lord gives the order to do the work of an ācārya.”
  30. Heading in the edition: “The deed of a Gauḍīya devotee: suddenly washing the Lord’s feet, he drinks that water.”
  31. Heading in the edition: “The anger of the Lord, who plays the part of an ācārya, the teacher of the world.”

  33. Anubhāṣya (on 126–127): for a jīva, the Lord’s eternal servant, to have his feet washed in the Lord’s temple is an offence in service, a breach of the rules of reverence (Hari-bhakti-vilāsa). No offence can be ascribed to the Lord, who is Bhagavān Himself; but acting as the teacher of the world, He took the part of an ordinary jīva to guard foolish would-be gurus against such offences.
  34. Pānā is a sweet drink (cf. Madhya 6.44). Heading in the edition: “The penalty for whoever gathers the least: he must treat the others to prasāda.”
  35. Heading in the edition: “The Guṇḍicā temple cleansed spotless.” Cf. 105, 106 and verse 1.
  36. Anubhāṣya: by the pastime of cleansing the Guṇḍicā temple Mahāprabhu, the teacher of the world, teaches that whoever wishes to seat Śrī Kṛṣṇa on the throne of his heart must first cleanse the heart, making it pure, calm and bright with devotion. The thorny grass, dust and pebbles are other desires and the pursuit of karma and of impersonal liberation; the fine stains the Lord rubbed away with His own cloth are hypocrisy, the craving for honour and gain, and finally the desire for liberation. The temple was cleansed to loud kīrtana of Kṛṣṇa’s name, and the Lord Himself taught each one how to serve.
  37. Amṛta-pravāha-bhāṣya: near the Guṇḍicā temple stands a beautiful old temple of Nṛsiṁha, where a great festival is held on Nṛsiṁha-caturdaśī.

  40. Amṛta-pravāha-bhāṣya (on 151–152): near the Guṇḍicā temple lies the Indradyumna lake; the Lord bathed in it, bowed down to Nṛsiṁhadeva and went into the garden.
  41. Anubhāṣya: piṇḍā (an Oriyā word) is a wooden seat.
  42. Heading in the edition: “Haridāsa’s natural humility and his reverence for the pure devotees.”
  43. Heading in the edition: “The Lord restrains Himself and His feelings.”

Amṛta-pravāha-bhāṣya: lāphrā is a plain vegetable dish, like a simple caccarī, which is mixed with rice and given out to the poor; amṛta-guṭikā are thick purīs soaked in thickened milk, commonly called amṛta-rasāvalī.
  45. The subject of the first line is not named; from 170 and 172 (tāṅra āge, “in front of him”) it is Jagadānanda, watching whether the Lord eats. Heading in the edition: “Fearing Jagadānanda’s displeasure, the Lord eats a little at a time.”

  47. Anubhāṣya: the bahirmukha, “those turned outward”, are those who think themselves enjoyers of outer forms and tastes, are busy gratifying their senses and have turned away from Kṛṣṇa’s service (cf. Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, 7.5.30–31).
  48. Heading in the edition: “A sannyāsī is not defiled by food.”
  49. Amṛta-pravāha-bhāṣya: the faults of food do not cling to a sannyāsī.
  50. Heading in the edition: “By calling himself a ‘householder brāhmaṇa’, Advaita feigns to follow the worldly society of the smārtas.”
  51. The words play on Advaita’s name. Anubhāṣya: in the guise of blame Nityānanda praises Advaita. Outwardly the non-dual knowledge Śrī Advaita preached may seem one with the māyāvādīs’ doctrine of merging into Brahman; but he is called Ācārya because he proclaims pure bhakti, and his “doctrine of non-duality” is the worship of non-dual knowledge, that is, pure bhakti. What Nityānanda condemns is the doctrine of exclusive non-duality (kevala-advaita), which obstructs pure bhakti (see also Madhya 3.93–101).
  52. Anubhāṣya: in the guise of blaming Advaita, Nityānanda describes the glory of non-dual knowledge. The supreme reality is the one Śrī Kṛṣṇa, and to see a “second” besides Him is māyā; the mahā-bhāgavata, like Prahlāda, sees only the one Kṛṣṇa. Pure Vaiṣṇavas accept the Truth as non-dual, but not as impersonal: it is Bhagavān, full of rasa, eternally with His name, form, qualities, pastimes and associates.
  53. Anubhāṣya: by this Nityānanda hints that a pure devotee should never eat together with a covert māyāvādī or a prākṛta-sahajiyā.
  54. Amṛta-pravāha-bhāṣya: vyāja-stuti is speech that blames outwardly but inwardly tells of greatness.
  55. Amṛta-pravāha-bhāṣya: the prasāda was sprinkled with the nectar of the Lord’s mercy, and so it became all the more delicious.
  56. Amṛta-pravāha-bhāṣya: this is what the pastime of cleansing the Guṇḍicā temple is called in the language of Utkala.
  57. Amṛta-pravāha-bhāṣya: during the Snāna-yātrā the paint on Jagannātha is washed off, and in the period of anavasara the bodies of the three Deities are painted anew (aṅgarāga); on the morning of the Nava-yauvana day comes the Netrotsava, the painting of the eyes. Anubhāṣya: Netrotsava, “the festival of the eyes”, is the first darśana after the two weeks of anavasara, when the eyes of those longing for darśana find their fulfilment.
  58. Anubhāṣya: karaṅga is the water pot of a sannyāsī. Heading in the edition: “In front of the Lord goes the strong Kāśīśvara, behind Him Govinda.”

Anubhāṣya (on 210–211): Mahāprabhu always looked at Jagannātha from the edge of the Jagamohana, from behind the Garuḍa pillar; but after two weeks of separation He went past it into the bhoga-maṇḍapa. To come so close to the worshipful is what is meant by breaking the rules (maryādā). Amṛta-pravāha-bhāṣya: maryādā is the rule of scripture for receiving darśana of the Deity.

  61. Amṛta-pravāha-bhāṣya: nīlamaṇi — His cheeks glistened like a mirror of sapphire (indranīla-maṇi).
  62. Anubhāṣya: bāndhulī here is the red flower of that kind; suraṅga is the colour of vermilion.
  63. Anubhāṣya: the longer Mahāprabhu gazed at the holy face, the stronger His thirst to see it grew, and between His eyes and Kṛṣṇa’s lotus face no difference or barrier remained. On the sweetness of the Deity see Śrī Rūpa’s Laghu-bhāgavatāmṛta and Śrīmad-Bhāgavatam, 10.29.14.
  64. Heading in the edition: “Though overwhelmed by feeling, the Lord restrains Himself and tastes the joy of serving by seeing.” Anubhāṣya: see Ādi 4.201–203.
  65. Heading in the edition: “In the joy of serving Kṛṣṇa by seeing Him the Lord forgets Himself; at last He returns home.”
  66. Heading in the edition: “By hearing the pastime of cleansing the Guṇḍicā temple even the impure are purified at heart.”
